articles_hidden.title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
articles_hidden.authors: Yiming Lu, Tingyu Lu, Di Zhang, Lili Ye, Hao Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.

articles_hidden.title: GTP orchestrates CTP synthase via an allosteric effector–cycling mechanism
articles_hidden.authors: Chen-Jun Guo, Yu-Fen Wu, Shu-Ying Guo, Jia-Li Lu, Liang Xu, You Fu, Xian Zhou, Jiale Zhong, Zherong Zhang, Ji-Long Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Cytidine triphosphate (CTP), a fundamental building block of RNA, plays vital roles in diverse biological processes. CTP synthase (CTPS) is the only known enzyme for de novo synthesis of CTP. Efficient CTPS catalysis requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) in a dose-dependent, nonconsumptive manner; however, the precise mechanism by which GTP drives CTP formation remains unclear. Here, we integrate a series of cryo-EM structures of Drosophila melanogaster CTPS captured from actively catalyzing samples with biochemical and mutagenesis analyses, yielding 34 distinct CTPS states at resolutions up to 2.0 Å. We find that GTP binds to and dissociates from CTPS once per catalytic cycle, thereby enabling the production of a single CTP molecule. Initial GTP engagement requires formation of 4-phosphoryl-UTP in the AL domain, whereas full stabilization of GTP binding is promoted by occupancy of the GAT active site. Together, these two checkpoints couple GTP recruitment and stabilization to catalytic progress in the two domains, enabling the coordinated synthesis of one CTP molecule per GTP binding–dissociation cycle. Moreover, the GTP-recognition site is highly conserved across the three domains of life. These findings establish a comprehensive mechanistic framework for efficient CTPS catalysis and define “effector-cycling”—in which GTP undergoes obligatory binding and dissociation during each catalytic cycle to regulate an intermediate step in a multistep catalytic process—as a distinct mode of allosteric regulation.

articles_hidden.title: Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO 2 uptake by DAB1
articles_hidden.authors: Naiya R. Phillips, Luke M. Oltrogge, Jonathan P. Remis, David F. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: CO 2 transporters enable bacterial CO 2 -concentrating mechanisms by catalyzing directional hydration of CO 2 , yet the basis of this vectorial carbonic anhydrase (CA) activity remains an open question. We used cryoelectron microscopy to determine the structure of the DAB1 complex from Thermocrinis albus to 2.29 Å, revealing a heterotrimer in which a deeply buried β-CA active site in DabA is structurally coupled to the proton-translocating subunit DabB. Two conformational states define distinct solvent channels for substrate entry and product exit. A suppressor screen identifies mutations that disrupt coupling while retaining CA activity, underlying the importance of conserved residues that link proton translocation to active-site remodeling. These results support a model in which proton-driven conformational changes regulate substrate access to the active site, enabling vectorial CO 2 hydration.

articles_hidden.title: Thermodynamic origin of atmospheric new particle formation: Theory for stable nucleating pairs
articles_hidden.authors: Roope Halonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Atmospheric new particle formation (NPF) has been observed across virtually all tropospheric environments, yet the meteorological conditions that favor or suppress it have resisted clear theoretical resolution. Here we show that, for neutral chemistries in which a strongly bound molecular pair constitutes the critical cluster, the thermodynamic precondition for NPF is set by a single quantity: the effective binding free energy of that pair, Δ G AB ° ( T , RH ) , which captures the competing influences of temperature and relative humidity in a closed-form analytical framework. Applied to the sulfuric acid–dimethylamine system in the boundary layer, the theory reproduces observed clustering across laboratory experiments and field campaigns spanning a polluted megacity, a remote high-altitude site, and an ultra-pristine boreal peatland, all without kinetic fitting parameters; precursor concentrations and the condensation sink enter as separable factors that govern the subsequent production rate. The framework reveals an optimal Δ G AB ° that maximizes cluster production, providing a thermodynamic basis for why NPF peaks at midday, favors spring over other seasons, occurs under heat wave conditions despite temperatures approaching + 40 ° C, and can even arise on rare evenings in near-pristine conditions. More broadly, the theory exposes the inherent relationship between atmospheric conditions and the earliest steps of particle formation, offering a general interpretive tool that complements and extends what observations and simulations alone cannot provide.

articles_hidden.title: Microbial niche partitioning explains N 2 O distributions and cycling in marine oxygen minimum zones
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel McCoy, Xin Sun, Pearse J. Buchanan, Emily J. Zakem
articles_hidden.abstract: Oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) are marine hotspots for cycling and emission of the powerful greenhouse gas nitrous oxide (N 2 O). Steep redox gradients host diverse microbial communities that produce and consume N 2 O, generating a characteristic vertical distribution, with low concentrations in anoxic cores and supersaturated accumulation in surrounding oxyclines. Although the accumulation is commonly attributed to stronger O 2 inhibition of N 2 O consumption than production, this differential inhibition is not consistently observed, suggesting that interactions among nitrogen-cycling metabolisms may provide additional mechanisms. To evaluate the ecological controls on the N 2 O profile, we embed a trait-based ecosystem model into an eddy-resolving simulation of the Eastern Tropical South Pacific OMZ. In this framework, redox energetics, metabolite exchange, competition, and grazing structure microbial growth, setting emergent niches of microbial functional types, particularly aerobic ammonia oxidizers and diverse anaerobic denitrifiers that mediate N 2 O cycling. In the anoxic core, cross-feeding tightly couples denitrifiers that produce and consume N 2 O, maintaining low concentrations. As O 2 increases in the oxycline, competition with aerobic metabolisms and intensified grazing gradually exclude denitrifiers. However, because they draw on more abundant substrates, N 2 O-producing denitrifiers persist to higher O 2 than N 2 O consumers, reflecting the vulnerability of populations dependent on intermediate metabolites. This ecological decoupling drives N 2 O accumulation and captures the characteristic double-peaked vertical structure without imposing physiological O 2 intolerance thresholds. More broadly, by revealing how niche partitioning and producer–consumer coupling shape other features of OMZ biogeochemistry, these results provide a basis for projecting future shifts in marine nitrogen loss and N 2 O emissions.

articles_hidden.title: Cell identity competes with surface tension to determine stromal organization in tumor spheroids beyond the CAF shell paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Claire Wilhelm
articles_hidden.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often found forming a peripheral stromal barrier around tumors. Here, this paradigm is challenged using microfabricated 3D cancer–CAF spheroid models combined with quantitative magnetic force tensiometry. A surface tension atlas is established for eight cancer cell lines, three CAF populations, and heterotypic tumor–CAF assemblies, spanning nearly two orders of magnitude. Surface tension is first shown to govern spheroid morphology and modulate drug response. Besides, CAFs consistently occupy the highest end of the surface tension hierarchy, predicting core rather than peripheral localization and directly challenging the shell paradigm. Yet confocal imaging reveals not only central accumulation but also complete CAF-tumor mixing, including in spheroids where cancer cells exhibit surface tensions nearly two orders of magnitude lower than CAFs. Surface tension alone therefore fails to predict CAF organization. Instead, the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) state of cancer cells emerges as a major determinant: epithelial-like tumors promote CAF core accumulation, whereas mesenchymal-like states favor persistent mixing. Peripheral CAF localization emerges only under restricted conditions combining high tumor cohesion and sequential stromal recruitment. Together, these results identify surface tension, EMT state, and assembly chronology as joint determinants of tumor–stroma architecture, revealing a context-dependent organization landscape rather than a universal CAF shell.

articles_hidden.title: Imaging and recording of synaptic zinc in the brain by covalent chemistry–based semisynthetic biosensors
articles_hidden.authors: Hao Zhu, Seiji Sakamotob, Keisuke Nakamura, Chengli Qiu, Kohei Nakajima, Hiroshi Nonaka, Itaru Hamachi
articles_hidden.abstract: Labile zinc ions (Zn 2+ ) are stored in glutamatergic vesicles at specific excitatory synapses in the central nervous system and released into synaptic clefts in an activity-dependent manner. However, the precise roles of synaptic Zn 2+ remain unclear due to a lack of tools capable of analyzing Zn 2+ with synapse-level spatial resolution in vivo. Here, we developed neuroreceptor-based semisynthetic biosensors that function as integrating dosimeters, recording synaptic Zn 2+ by covalent chemistry in the living mouse brain. Using a chemical knock-in strategy, we introduced activity-based Zn 2+ probes with distinct affinities into endogenous α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole-propionic acid or γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors. These in-brain-constructed Zn 2+ sensors enabled region-specific mapping of Zn 2+ in synaptic clefts in the living mouse brain. Imaging-based analyses revealed differences in apparent Zn 2+ levels at excitatory and inhibitory synapses across hippocampal regions during kainate-induced seizures, providing insights into the physiological and pathological functions of synaptic Zn 2+ .

articles_hidden.title: Superconductivity in the high-pressure tetragonal phase of UTe 2
articles_hidden.authors: Yuhang Deng, Gabriel Mee, Tyler Wannamaker, Keke Feng, Mingyu Xu, Weiwei Xie, M. Brian Maple
articles_hidden.abstract: Electrical transport and magnetic measurements have been made on UTe 2 under pressure P up to ~16 GPa to determine the superconducting transition temperature T c vs. P phase diagram in the high-pressure tetragonal phase. Superconductivity emerges near ~5 GPa, coincident with the orthorhombic—tetragonal phase transition; in the tetragonal phase, T c reaches a maximum value of ~4 K at 6 GPa and then decreases with P and appears to vanish near 18 GPa. Tetragonal UTe 2 has a relatively small upper critical field H c2 (0) ≈ 1.2 T at 5.3 GPa, smaller than the Pauli paramagnetic limit, and is orbitally limited with a coherence length ξ tetra ≈ 16.5 nm. This small value of H c2 (0) favors more conventional superconductivity; in contrast, the large values of H c2 ( T ) for orthorhombic UTe 2 exceed the Pauli paramagnetic limit in all three crystallographic directions and have been attributed to unconventional superconductivity, widely believed to involve spin-triplet pairing. The temperature–pressure phase diagram of UTe 2 shows a striking dichotomy: a narrow, fragile, unconventional superconducting region in the orthorhombic phase vs. a broad, robust, and more conventional superconducting dome in the tetragonal phase. This dichotomy is consistent with the proposal that U-dimers, present (absent) in the orthorhombic (tetragonal) phase, may play a role in spin-triplet superconductivity of orthorhombic UTe 2 . In the tetragonal phase, the normal-state electrical resistivity ρ( T ) exhibits metallic behavior with a “knee” at 200 to 240 K that depends weakly on P and most likely marks the onset of a transition to a magnetically ordered phase that coexists with superconductivity.

articles_hidden.title: A Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex drives enhanced depotentiation in a mouse model of improved cognitive flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Cole Malloy, Jia-Hua Hu, Ying Liu, Meghyn A. Welch, Mumeko C. Tsuda, Heather A. Cameron, Dax A. Hoffman
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory updating promotes cognitive flexibility by enabling suppression of outdated information to optimize behavioral strategies in response to a changing environment. While some circuits involved have been identified, the synaptic mechanisms underlying this process remain uncertain. Here, using a recently developed Kv4.2 knock-in mouse model (Kv4.2TA), we identify a metaplasticity in the hippocampus that accompanies an improvement in cognitive flexibility. Mutation of a C-terminal phosphorylation site (T607) in the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated K + channel protein Kv4.2 drives boosted depotentiation of spike timing-dependent long-term synaptic potentiation mediated by mGluR5 receptors, putative constituents of Kv4.2 macromolecular complexes. We found that mGluR5 receptors are required for the improved cognitive flexibility observed in Kv4.2TA mice. These findings reveal a synaptic correlate associated with memory updating in cognitive flexibility and spotlight the Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex as a therapeutic target for disorders characterized by impairments in cognitive flexibility.

articles_hidden.title: Drivers of the likelihood of evolutionary rescue in response to novel infectious diseases
articles_hidden.authors: Laurinne J. Balstad, Marissa L. Baskett
articles_hidden.abstract: The introduction of novel infectious diseases has caused significant declines in many species, and in some cases, local extinction. Simultaneously, hosts might adapt to these novel pathogens, allowing population recovery, an example of evolutionary rescue (ER). Novel infectious diseases differ from sudden, abiotic stressors in that disease only impacts a subset of individuals within the population and individuals might be affected for a finite period. Whether ER occurs in an infectious disease context, and how likely it is relative to abiotic stress, might depend on both host and pathogen characteristics such as the scale of transmission (e.g., local density-dependent transmission only or additional infection through an external reservoir), the degree of fatality or immunity, and the adaptive pathway in terms of whether adaptive alleles reduce mortality, reduce likelihood of infection, or enhance recovery. Here, we use a stochastic mathematical model of host-pathogen dynamics with evolution of a novel allele conferring disease robustness to quantify how population trajectories, including the probability of and time to ER, vary across adaptive pathways and disease characteristics. We find that ER is more likely to occur with dynamical disease transmission compared to a lasting stressor that affects the entire population, indicating that protecting a subset of the population from stress facilitates ER. Among cases with disease transmission, ER is generally more likely to occur with the adaptation of mortality-blocking alleles and sources of transmission that include an external reservoir.

articles_hidden.title: Changing contributions of emotion and reward information to learning through adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Camille V. Phaneuf-Hadd, Elizabeth A. Phelps, Leah H. Somerville
articles_hidden.abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8 to 22 y completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

articles_hidden.title: Competing presynaptic protein assemblies coordinate basal neurotransmission with homeostatic plasticity
articles_hidden.authors: Wen-Chieh Hsieh, Tae Hee Han, Rosario Vicidomini, Peter Nguyen, Mihaela Serpe
articles_hidden.abstract: Neural circuits establish a stable basal level of synaptic transmission that is maintained throughout life. When synaptic activity is perturbed, homeostatic mechanisms restore this set point, but how neurons reconcile long-term stability and rapid compensatory plasticity remains unclear. Here, we identify two competing presynaptic multimolecular complexes that control steady-state transmission and homeostatic potentiation and define the molecular switch that enables transitions between these functional states. At Drosophila neuromuscular junction, the transmembrane protein PlexinB (PlexB) and the auxiliary subunit Neto-α regulate both basal synaptic function and homeostatic plasticity. PlexB association with presynaptic KaiR1D/Neto-α receptor complexes modulates channel properties and fine-tunes neurotransmitter release, whereas PlexB signaling with Semaphorin2b (Sema2b) and Neto-α drives homeostatic potentiation. KaiR1D and Sema2b/PlexB compete for a limited pool of presynaptic Neto-α. Motor neurons switch from steady-state transmission to homeostatic potentiation by exchanging KaiR1D/Neto-α/PlexB complexes for Neto-α/PlexB/Sema2b. Critically, Neto-α must dissociate from KaiR1D-containing complexes to initiate the homeostatic response. Variants of Neto-α or KaiR1D that fail to dissociate support normal basal neurotransmission but abolish homeostatic plasticity. These findings demonstrate that dynamic reorganization of competing presynaptic protein assemblies enables neurons to preserve stable baseline transmission while mounting robust compensatory responses to perturbations. Given the widespread roles of presynaptic receptors and Semaphorin/Plexin signaling in synaptic regulation, this mechanism may represent a conserved strategy for balancing stability and plasticity in neural circuits.

articles_hidden.title: Invariances in an ever-variant environment
articles_hidden.authors: Priyom Adhyapok, Stefano Di Talia

articles_hidden.title: Evolution shapes ecosystem resilience through spatial self-organization
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaoli Dong, Alexander J. Richardson, Rachata Muneepeerakul
articles_hidden.abstract: Drylands are globally widespread and ecologically important but vulnerable to climate change. Many exhibit spatially self-organized vegetation patterns that enhance resilience by enabling vegetation to reorganize their patterns under drying, thereby optimizing water use and maintaining productivity. Plants can also undergo evolution in response to environmental change. Although both spatial self-organization and rapid evolution are fundamental mechanisms of resilience, their interaction remains largely unknown. Using a theoretical model, we examine how these mechanisms interact to shape vegetation transitions—abrupt or gradual—and ecosystem resilience under climatic drying. We find that pattern formation can suppress adaptation by maintaining soil moisture beneath vegetation patches despite rainfall decline, thereby limiting selection for increased drought tolerance. However, this suppression is largely alleviated under the variable rainfall typical of drylands. In turn, evolution feeds back on self-organization by increasing the spatial plasticity of vegetation patterns and their ability to reorganize under changing climate, although this positive effect weakens as evolutionary rate increases. Considering direct (adaptation) and indirect (pattern-mediated) effects, evolution enhances resilience, with indirect effects via pattern plasticity dominating. Within model scenarios spanning plausible rainfall variability and relative evolutionary-to-ecological rates, more than half of vegetation transitions are abrupt involving biomass losses exceeding 50%, highlighting a potential mechanism underlying recent global observations of widespread abrupt vegetation losses in drylands. These results demonstrate that evolution and spatial self-organization jointly determine dryland resilience under environmental change and highlight the unexpected role of evolution in patterned landscapes, calling for integrative approaches to predict ecosystem responses in a changing world.

articles_hidden.title: A GPRC5B–Fyn signaling axis regulates VRAC activity by targeting LRRC8A
articles_hidden.authors: Yulia Kostritskaia, Héctor Gaitán-Peñas, Sara Bertelli, Marta Alonso-Gardón, Malte Klüssendorf, Aida Castellanos, Guillem Pont-Espinós, Adrià Pla-Casillanis, Marc González-Subías, Ekaitz Errasti-Murugarren, Tania López-Hernández, Michael Pusch, Tobias Stauber, Raúl Estévez
articles_hidden.abstract: The mechanisms by which physiological signals gate the volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a GPRC5B–Fyn signaling axis that directly controls VRAC activation by targeting the essential subunit LRRC8A. We found that the orphan G protein–coupled receptor GPRC5B binds LRRC8A and recruits the Src family kinase Fyn, which in turn suppresses hypotonicity-evoked VRAC activation. Disrupting Fyn binding to GPRC5B or substituting a predicted phosphorylation site on LRRC8A (Y362) abolishes this inhibition. Across primary astrocytes and reconstituted systems, GPRC5B prevents the intersubunit conformational rearrangements associated with VRAC opening without altering basal channel expression. In astrocytes, the MLC protein MLC1 partially sequesters GPRC5B, thereby reducing the GPRC5B–LRRC8A interaction, providing a mechanistic link to VRAC dysfunction in megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy. These results reveal a receptor-kinase-channel pathway that gates VRAC through Y362-dependent modulation of LRRC8A, establishing a molecular framework for VRAC regulation and its disruption in disease.

articles_hidden.title: The honey bee stinger: An unusual pump with collapsible double pistons
articles_hidden.authors: Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel, Claudia Klose, Hyun Chai Lee, Quinn Graco, Ajay Narendra, Sridhar Ravi
articles_hidden.abstract: Most stinging animals deliver venom by contracting muscles around a venom reservoir, but honey bees employ a fundamentally different strategy. The stingers of worker bees have the unique ability to autotomize, separating from the body, to continue to sting independently. Despite more than a century of anatomical descriptions, the mechanics of venom pumping have remained unresolved due to the challenges of observing them in action. We recorded high-speed videos of active, autotomized stingers, combined with micro computed tomography-based three-dimensional reconstruction to characterize the biomechanics of stinging in the honey bee Apis mellifera . We reveal that the stinger functions as a unique double-piston micro-pump. Two lancets, each possessing a deformable valve, slide in antiphase within a bulb chamber. These valves dynamically deform to alternately form a seal during the downstroke and collapse during the upstroke, enabling pressure generation for pumping while potentially minimizing backflow during refilling. The inverted tear-drop shape of the bulb facilitates refill even while pumping proceeds. We explored valve deformations and flow behavior by constructing a dynamically scaled physical model of the bulb chamber confirming key features of the pumping cycle and propose mechanisms for valve deformations. The double piston design adds significant design complexity but enables continuous venom delivery in a compact, autonomous unit. These findings provide deeper understanding of venom pumping in honey bees and other Hymenoptera. This study also provides evidence of an axial piston pump within a biological system and offers inspiration for the design of microfluidic pumping devices.

articles_hidden.title: Interfacial microenvironments enable abiotic ribonucleoside formation in micro- and nanoscale compartments
articles_hidden.authors: Qiang Liu, Xia Zhao, Jae Kyoo Lee, Richard N. Zare
articles_hidden.abstract: The abiotic emergence of ribonucleosides remains a central challenge in origin-of-life research because ribonucleosides form inefficiently and are often unstable under prebiotically plausible conditions. Here we show that interfacial microenvironments within aqueous micro- and nanoscale compartments containing D-ribose, phosphoric acid, and nucleobases promote ribonucleoside formation by creating reaction-permissive physicochemical conditions independent of the specific compartment type. Across a diverse range of compartmentalized systems, including gas–oil–water micro/nanobubbles, gas–water micro/nanobubbles, microscale lipid-bilayer vesicles, and oil–water emulsion systems, ribonucleosides form abiotically in the absence of enzymatic catalysis. Under selected interfacial conditions, multiple ribonucleosides, including cytidine, are generated without added catalysts. Comparison among these systems reveals that interfacial architecture and coupled physicochemical properties strongly influence both reaction efficiency and product stability. CO 2 -based micro/nanobubbles support sustained cytidine accumulation, highlighting the importance of coupled gas–liquid and liquid–liquid interfaces. Ribonucleoside synthesis also depends on compartment size, whereas variations in oil content within micro/nanobubbles selectively modulate inosine formation, underscoring the sensitivity of nucleoside chemistry to interfacial properties. These findings identify interfacial microenvironments within micro- and nanoscale compartments as a general physical framework for ribonucleoside emergence and suggest that ubiquitous compartmentalized interfaces on early Earth could have provided robust settings for prebiotic ribonucleoside chemistry.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of modulator therapy on the Pseudomonas aeruginosa cystic fibrosis lung transcriptome
articles_hidden.authors: Morgana Letizia, Lauren E. Whiteley, Frances L. Diggle, Angela N. Davis, Sarah J. Morgan, Brenda Grogan, John Baugh, Edward F. McKone, Pradeep K. Singh, Marvin Whiteley
articles_hidden.abstract: Chronic lung infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major complication of cystic fibrosis (CF), contributing to lung function decline and increased morbidity and mortality. Laboratory models are used to study CF infections, but their relevance depends on how accurately they reproduce microbial physiology during human infection. We previously developed a framework that uses bacterial gene expression in human infections to quantify model accuracy. Here, we applied this framework to determine how a major therapeutic intervention impacts P. aeruginosa physiology in the lungs of people with CF (pwCF) and to develop and evaluate refined preclinical models. We focused on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), a highly effective CFTR modulator therapy that has improved outcomes for pwCF. However, evidence indicates that P. aeruginosa lung infections persist despite ETI therapy. Analysis of P. aeruginosa transcriptomes from human sputum collected before and after ETI initiation revealed minimal changes in gene expression, indicating that the CF airway continues to support a similar bacterial transcriptional state despite therapy. We then evaluated how strain selection, zinc limitation, and polymicrobial coculture influence the ability of laboratory models to recapitulate P. aeruginosa gene expression in human CF sputum. Growth of CF clinical isolates in zinc-limited synthetic CF sputum medium produced the most accurate model, whereas population-based cultures and coculture with Staphylococcus aureus had limited effects. These findings show that ETI therapy has little impact on the conserved P. aeruginosa transcriptional state in human CF sputum and that refined sputum-like models remain useful for studying persistent infection in the postmodulator era.

articles_hidden.title: IGF2BP1 in 17q-gain cooperates with MYCN to regulate purine biosynthesis and immunotherapy efficacy in neuroblastoma
articles_hidden.authors: Jiaxu Liu, Yingzhe Fang, Rongrong Fan, Honghong Wang, Hao Huang, Fan Yang, Lihui Yu, Zhinang Yin, Mingyue Zhao, Pingping Zeng, Ganggang Song, Yu Liu, Jinfang Zhang, Qianqian Yuan, Kaiwei Liang, Baishan Jiang, Hudan Liu, Guoliang Qing
articles_hidden.abstract: Concurrent chromosomal 17q-gain and MYCN amplification define a subset of neuroblastoma associated with particularly adverse clinical outcomes. However, how these genetic alterations synergize to promote tumor progression and whether their cooperation confers therapeutic vulnerabilities remain elusive. We herein performed a CRISPR-based functional screen targeting 17q-gain genes and identified the RNA m 6 A reader IGF2BP1 as a critical MYCN collaborator to promote aggressive neuroblastomas via activation of phosphoribosylaminoimidazole succinocarboxamide synthetase (PAICS), a key enzyme involved in de novo purine biosynthesis. Rewiring of PAICS-mediated nucleotide metabolism enabled tumor cells to sustain necessary purine pools for productive transcription of replicative stress-responsive genes, including CHK1 , to cope with the exacerbated replication stress. Pharmacological inhibition of CHK1 elicited a robust immune reprogramming, leading to activation of cGAS–STING signaling, upregulation of Major Histocompatibility Complex class I expression, and synergistic tumor suppression with immune checkpoint blockade. Altogether, we identify an IGF2BP1/MYCN–PAICS–CHK1 axis that drives aggressive neuroblastoma phenotypes and constitutes an actionable vulnerability for therapeutic intervention.

articles_hidden.title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation
articles_hidden.authors: Chung-Ta Han, Karen Tsay, Samuel Lobo, Saeed Najafi, Kieran Monahan, Erica Hong, M. Scott Shell, Joan-Emma Shea, Songi Han
articles_hidden.abstract: Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation water has been proposed to be a signature of such hot spots at both the tau fibril-end surface and soluble tau monomers. Although jR2R3-P301L tau exhibits a heterogeneous hydration landscape in its intrinsically disordered state, with enhanced water structuring near the P301L mutation site, it is unclear whether a localized hotspot exists at the fibril end surface and surface water facilitates the initial contacts in templated aggregation. Using rapid 1 H- 15 N SOFAST-HMQC NMR to track seed-induced aggregation of jR2R3-P301L in real time, complemented by molecular dynamics simulation of fibril surface hydration, we identify a residue-specific pinning hotspot that is prone to dewetting followed by sequential folding and incorporation of the remaining segment in a two-step dock-and-lock process. Site-specific spin labeling further demonstrates that blocking this pinning hotspot disrupts templated aggregation, leading to shorter fibrils. The identification of a dominant pinning site will facilitate the rational design of binders to effectively disrupt fibril extension or serve as diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Direct physical contacts with epithelial cells regulate leukocyte actin dynamics to facilitate intraepithelial motility in vivo
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan H. Schrope, Tanner F. Robertson, Adam Horn, Jack J. Stevens, Clyde W. Tinnen, Julie Rindy, Nicholas Garcia, Yiran Hou, Emilie Rochon, David J. Beebe, Anna Huttenlocher
articles_hidden.abstract: Efficient immune cell migration requires physical interactions with surrounding tissues. While tissue matrix mechanics influence leukocyte motility, it is unknown how leukocytes exert pushing and pulling forces to traverse cell-dense epithelial tissues in vivo. Here, we leverage the optical transparency of larval zebrafish to identify how physical interactions with epithelial cells regulate mechanisms of neutrophil force generation to navigate cell-dense tissues. Confining forces from epithelial cells induce a mechanosensitive central actin network, mediated by Cdc42 and Wiskott–Aldrich Syndrome Protein, which exerts expansile forces on surrounding cells to dilate a path for migration. In concert, direct cell-to-cell (leukocyte–epithelial) contacts mediated by integrin ɑE recognition of epithelial cadherin generate traction forces to enable forward motility. Together, our findings identify how physical interactions with the surrounding cellular environment regulate leukocyte motility through epithelial tissue in vivo.

articles_hidden.title: How biological synapses self-assemble gradient learning
articles_hidden.authors: Qianli Liao, Liu Ziyin, Yulu Gan, Brian Cheung, Mark T. Harnett, Tomaso Poggio
articles_hidden.abstract: Existing models of learning in the brain explain how given circuits learn, but not how biology could assemble those circuits in the first place. To address this gap, we formulate Self-Assembling Learning—the study of how learning systems can emerge from lower-level interactions—and introduce one example mechanism, the Self-Assembling Motif (SAM). SAM is self-assembling at two scales: The motif emerges from initially random connectivity under heterosynaptic plasticity rules, and networks of SAMs, composed hierarchically, self-organize into dynamics that provably approximate a generalized form of stochastic gradient descent—matching backpropagation-level performance. This suggests that biological learning need not be prescribed but can emerge from local rules—and to a far greater extent than previously thought.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental chemical mixtures reprogram mammary epithelial development to epigenetic states associated with breast cancer
articles_hidden.authors: Meadow Parrish, Meloryn Seraj, Helia Nikoueian, Nicole Traugh, Andrew Chen, Piyush B. Gupta, Stefano Monti, Charlotte Kuperwasser
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental exposures occur as complex mixtures, yet the mechanisms by which they alter human tissue development and generate cancer-relevant tissue states remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a physiologically relevant 3D human breast organoid high-content screening platform that relates exposure-induced developmental disruption to cancer-relevant cell states. Screening of structurally diverse environmental chemicals as single agents and mixtures reveals heterogeneous but reproducible developmental responses, indicating that distinct environmental chemicals perturb different aspects of mammary morphogenesis. Focusing on bisphenols, we show that a low-dose mixture (BPA, BPS, and BPF; 3BPX) disrupts organoid development and induces transcriptional programs characterized by extracellular matrix remodeling, epithelial plasticity, and partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition, accompanied by widespread DNA methylation remodeling. A 3BPX exposure signature maps to ER+ luminal breast cancers and is preferentially enriched in invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC), a subtype characterized by epithelial plasticity. The 3BPX-associated methylation signature is detectable in primary tumors and adjacent normal tissue and is enriched in ILC. Together, these findings show that environmentally relevant chemical mixtures induce heterogeneous developmental perturbations that converge on conserved transcriptional and epigenetic programs associated with epithelial plasticity and tissue remodeling. These exposure-associated signatures are represented in defined epithelial and stromal compartments in human breast cancers, supporting a model in which developmental exposures may establish field-like, cancer-relevant tissue states.

articles_hidden.title: Two clusters of brain regions with distinct age-related profiles of functional connectivity in autism spectrum disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Xinrui Li, Fengzhu Zuo, Yi Cheng, Kyle Perkins, Fan Cao
articles_hidden.abstract: Brain functional connectivity changes throughout development, and individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may follow trajectories that differ from those of typically developing controls. Using large multisite resting-state fMRI cross-sectional datasets, we examined how functional connectivity differences between ASD and typically developing controls change across a broad age range of 5 to 64 y. A data-driven analysis identified two spatially distributed clusters of cortical regions showing distinct age-related profiles of ASD–TD connectivity differences. Cluster 1 was marked by consistent hypoconnectivity across ages, suggesting a stable neural signature of ASD. Cluster 2 was characterized by hypoconnectivity in childhood that gradually diminished with age, suggesting a temporary delay profile. These clusters were systematically organized along the sensory–association axis. Cluster 1 mainly involved lower-rank sensory and sensorimotor cortices, while Cluster 2 mainly involved higher-rank association cortices. Brain–behavior analyses revealed greater and broader ASD symptom associations across ages in the consistent hypoconnectivity profile than the delay profile. Further subtype analyses suggested that social-affect symptoms were associated with greater hypoconnectivity than repetitive behavior symptoms in both clusters. Spatial correlation analyses with neurotransmitter maps revealed associations of Cluster 1 with mGluR5 and of Cluster 2 with GABA A α5, providing insight into the neurobiological basis of the two clusters. In a cross-disorder validation analysis, applying the same analytic framework to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder did not reveal comparable results. Together, these findings suggest that ASD-related functional connectivity alterations are developmentally heterogeneous and organized along the cortical hierarchy, providing a developmental perspective for understanding the neurobiology of ASD.

articles_hidden.title: Nonclassical growth to mesoporous quasi-single crystal CeO 2 superstructures with a well-defined surface
articles_hidden.authors: Meiyang Cui, Xiangru Wei, Moon Young Yang, Grayson Johnson, Perrin Godbold, Yizhen Chen, Maoyu Wang, Yugang Zhang, Chang Liu, Shengsong Yang, Brian Lee, Sooyeon Hwang, Farzad Bastani, Mingyang Liu, Petra Reinke, Lu Ma, Hua Zhou, Christopher B. Murray, William A. Goddard, Sen Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Single-crystal materials are essential for fundamental catalysis studies and advanced technologies; however, synthesizing single crystals that simultaneously integrate mesoporosity, tunable size, and well-defined surfaces remains challenging. Here, we report a wet-chemical, template-free strategy to synthesize mesoporous quasi-single-crystal CeO 2 superparticles (SPs). Operando wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering combined with theoretical modeling reveal a nonclassical growth mechanism driven by the oriented attachment of nanocluster building blocks. This process yields high-surface-area quasi-single crystals that preferentially expose energetically favorable (111) facets on both the external surfaces and internal pore walls, thereby enhancing the stabilization of active sites when used as heterogeneous catalyst supports. Using this approach, we demonstrate broad applicability by synthesizing highly dispersed precious metal–loaded CeO 2 (M/CeO 2 , M = Pd, Pt, Rh, or Ir) and metal-doped CeO 2 (Cu–CeO 2 ) SPs. Moreover, Pd/CeO 2 SPs exhibit effective stabilization of Pd clusters in CO 2 hydrogenation to methanol, delivering a high methanol selectivity of 85% and markedly improved durability compared with conventional supports.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct functional open states of the polymodal nociceptor TRPV1
articles_hidden.authors: Bo Hyun Lee, Shisheng Li, Simon Vu, Zhihao Yao, Yuhua Tian, Vladimir Yarov-Yarovoy, Jie Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: The polymodal nociceptor TRPV1 integrates diverse physical and chemical stimuli, yet whether these inputs drive a common activated state remains unresolved. Here, we show that TRPV1 activators stabilize functionally distinct open states that yield discrete single-channel conductance levels. These functional states appear to arise from distinct open-pore conformations, as evidenced by anomalous mole fraction effect measurements. Structurally, stimulus-specific changes in pore conformation were directly observed using site-directed fluorescence recordings, consistent with Rosetta-guided structural models. Notably, coactivation by two stimuli markedly slows channel opening rather than producing synergistic acceleration, suggesting potential conformational incompatibility across subunits. Together, these findings define TRPV1 gating as a stimulus-partitioned, multistate process and highlight opportunities for selective modulation of TRPV1 in pain management.

articles_hidden.title: Abiotic conversion of nitrate to ammonium enhances nitrogen use efficiency in paddy soils
articles_hidden.authors: Chunlei Liu, Manting Wang, Hongzhe Li, Jianfei Li, Jingru Xu, Nan Zhang, Chao Zhu, Jun Shan, Guibing Zhu, Yong-Guan Zhu
articles_hidden.abstract: Nitrogen (N) use efficiency is critical in ensuring food production while reducing nitrate (NO 3 − -N) to ammonium (NH 4 + -N) is widely recognized as a key for reducing N loss from paddy fields. Microbial involvement has long been regarded as the indispensable step for NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N in nature; it remains largely unknown whether abiotic processes can drive this. Here, using laser confocal fluorescence microscopy and thermodynamic laws, we find that Fe(II) ions in the rice rhizosphere exist on iron plaque in a specific manner with strong reducing capability. These specifically adsorbed Fe(II) ions (Fe(II) SA ) could mediate the abiotic reduction of NO 3 − -N to NH 4 + -N, accounting for 57% of the total NO 3 − -N reduction. When cultured in a sterile nutrient solution containing only 15 NO 3 − -N and Fe(II) ions, over 90% of N in the xylem of rice plants exists as 15 NH 4 + -N, directly proving the occurrence of NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N and taken up by rice. Theoretical calculations elucidate the Fe(II) SA -induced local electron depolarization enhances interfacial charge transfer which drives this reaction with the conversion of *NO to *NOH/*NHO identified as the rate-limiting step. We then propose a regulatory strategy to establish a stable Fe(II) SA /Fe(III) SA cycle utilizing FeC for controlled-release of Fe(II) ions. Two-year field experiments confirmed this strategy can increase rice yield by 16.1% while cutting half of the N input. Our work enables the design of novel pathways in improving N use efficiency for sustainable rice production.

articles_hidden.title: Mechanistic versus descriptive interpretation of brain activity pattern reconstruction
articles_hidden.authors: Kyesam Jung, Simon B. Eickhoff, Kaustubh R. Patil
articles_hidden.abstract: The geometric eigenmodes, derived from the shape of the cortical surface, have been suggested as a better model for explaining brain function due to their high accuracy in reconstructing patterns of both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked brain activity patterns captured by functional MRI, when contrasted with alternative models including structural connectome derived bases. While a descriptive representation offers valuable utility for neuroimaging studies, it is necessary to examine the extent to which it supports a mechanistic explanation for human brain function. Although the observation that geometric eigenmodes accurately fit brain activity is intriguing, we argue that accepting them as a model of brain function risks conflating descriptive and mechanistic interpretations. While a representation that effectively describes the underlying geometry is inherently adept at fitting patterns within that geometric space; it does not necessarily shed light on mechanisms that give rise to the brain’s functional attributes. To this end, we provide two lines of empirical results: a) geometric eigenmodes demonstrate a high flexibility when fit to a range of manipulated patterns, and b) localized parcel-based representations can reconstruct activity patterns as well. Based on those results, theoretical considerations, and previous data, we argue that more consideration is needed regarding the complementary roles of descriptive representation and mechanistic explanation in neuroimaging research. While we recognize the potential role of the brain’s geometry in influencing its dynamics, assertions regarding its efficacy should be weighed against its inherent lack of specificity, biological interpretability, and anatomical evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Extensive glacier loss in the coterminous United States
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew G. Fountain, Bryce Glenn, Christopher McNeil, Brian Menounos
articles_hidden.abstract: Glaciers populate the mountain ranges of the western conterminous United States and despite their importance to alpine hydrology, their area and volume change have never been comprehensively evaluated. Our study shows that since the mid-twentieth century about one-quarter of the glaciers have disappeared and the overall area and volume are reduced by one-third. The pattern of glacier shrinkage suggests most glaciers in the conterminous United States are largely maintained by local topographic influences due to their small size. These results improve our understanding of evolving high alpine hydrology and importance to ecosystem processes.

articles_hidden.title: Field experiments predict ecological response to a large-scale epidemic of an anti-keystone pathogen
articles_hidden.authors: J. Timothy Wootton, Khashiff Miranda, Amy K. Henry, Catherine A. Pfister
articles_hidden.abstract: Knowledge of how pathogens, in the context of a changing environment, shape the structure of ecological communities remains limited, and little information exists on the ability of small-scale field experiments to predict the consequences of large-scale environmental impacts. We addressed these issues using the emergence of a widespread epidemic (sea star wasting disease, SSWD) on rocky intertidal shorelines. Prior experiments demonstrated strong reductions in sessile species diversity in response to the local experimental removal of the sea star Pisaster ochraceus [R. T. Paine, Am. Nat. 100 , 65–75 (1966); R. T. Paine, Oceologia 15 , 93–120 (1974)] at our site. In surveys of sea star populations over 8 y spanning the onset of the SSWD epidemic, P. ochraceus populations declined by 90%, then subsequently recovered to about one third of pre-epidemic size under an endemic disease phase. Using four different types of temporal data, we documented large increases in populations of the competitively dominant mussel Mytilus californianus following P. ochraceus decline, which were of similar magnitude to those observed in prior field experiments. As in the field experiments, sessile species richness and diversity declined strongly following the onset of the SSWD epidemic as mussels were released from predator control. Our results reveal a strong effect of a pathogen in regulating ecological community structure by disrupting the role of a keystone species, a result anticipated by prior small-scale field experiments.

articles_hidden.title: Astrocytic facilitation of somatic NMDARs underpins hippocampal E-S potentiation
articles_hidden.authors: Xi Dong, Zhaohui Chen, Yi Fu, Zhi Wang, Wei Lu
articles_hidden.abstract: EPSP–spike (E-S) potentiation is a form of plasticity defined by a persistent increase in neuronal spike output for a given synaptic input, reflecting enhanced E-S coupling independent of synaptic strength. However, its cellular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that brief induction of E-S potentiation triggers a sustained calcium activity increase in astrocytes adjacent to the hippocampal CA1 pyramidal layer. Mechanistically, E-S potentiation critically requires GluN2B-containing N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) localized to the neuronal soma. Sustained astrocytic activity promotes E-S potentiation through vesicular release of D-serine, which enhances tonic activation of somatic NMDARs, suppresses A-type potassium currents, and produces a lasting increase in neuronal excitability. Functionally, this astrocyte-dependent E-S potentiation lowers the threshold for subsequent long-term potentiation, conferring a metaplastic influence on hippocampal circuits. These findings identify an astrocyte-neuron signaling mechanism that drives intrinsic plasticity and establish somatic NMDARs as a key site of astrocytic regulation of hippocampal output.

articles_hidden.title: Global proteolysis during starvation governs proteome remodeling and a survival–regrowth trade-off in bacteria
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriel Manzanarez, Rohan Balakrishnan, Harish Kannan, Miriam Abele, Hiroyuki Okano, Fukang She, Zhongge Zhang, Chenhao Wu, Lance Freiman, Christina Ludwig, Matteo Mori, Terence Hwa
articles_hidden.abstract: Starving bacteria must synthesize stress proteins to survive, but how protein synthesis persists in the absence of nutrient influx is unclear. We show that in Escherichia coli , carbon starvation triggers large-scale proteome remodeling, with global proteolysis supplying both the amino acids (AAs) and ATP for protein synthesis. This remodeling occurs in two phases, with a short preparatory phase relying on constitutive proteolytic machinery and fueled by residual carbon waste, and a more extended phase, relying on starvation-induced protein components synthesized during the preparatory phase and fueled by AA catabolism. The starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) program dominating the extended phase depends on YeaG, a little-known, broadly conserved protein highly expressed in stationary phase under the control of the general stress sigma factor RpoS. SPD fuels the synthesis of stress proteins, including those in the RpoS regulon and AA catabolic enzymes, markedly enhancing survival and accounting for much of the viability benefit conferred by RpoS during carbon starvation. However, in mutants where an energy source can be supplemented without enabling biomass growth, SPD and the accompanying protein synthesis are largely dispensable for survival, indicating that a primary physiological function of the synthesized stress proteins is to conserve or recycle energy during carbon starvation. Because SPD targets biosynthetic enzymes nonspecifically, proteome remodeling via SPD imposes a fundamental trade-off between long-term survival and short-term metabolic activity, manifested as a lag before regrowth upon nutrient replenishment. Together, these findings establish SPD as a general physiological strategy shaping protein synthesis and survival in nongrowing bacteria.

articles_hidden.title: To reverse nature loss, change what drives it
articles_hidden.authors: David Cooper, Sandra Díaz
articles_hidden.abstract: This week, at the 17th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), delegates from 195 countries and the European Union are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, for a global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, an international set of goals and targets adopted in 2022 to tackle the biodiversity crisis. The urgent question before them is clear: What must change now to halt and reverse nature’s decline and put it on a path to recovery by 2030? COP-17 comes as international cooperation is under increasing strain. Extreme weather is intensifying, ecosystem deterioration is creating new security risks, and geopolitical tensions are rising. Yet nature’s decline does not pause for geopolitical instability—it deepens it. That makes effective multilateralism, with North and South as equal partners, more important, not less.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis for size-selective perception of chitin in plants
articles_hidden.authors: Kira Gysel, Simon Boje Hansen, Henriette Rübsam, Husam M. A. B. Alsarraf, Eva Madland, Caroline Baadegaard, Ebbe Engholm, Jeryl Xin Jie Cheng, Emil Christian Poulsen, Maria Vinther, Knud Jørgen Jensen, Mikkel Boas Thygesen, Sebastien Fort, Jens Stougaard, Kasper Røjkjær Andersen
articles_hidden.abstract: Plants detect microbes through pattern recognition receptors that perceive conserved microbial surface motifs known as microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs). Lysin motif (LysM) receptors recognize and mediate downstream responses to chitinous MAMPs. In this study, we elucidated the mechanism for the specific recognition of long-chain chitin oligomers and identified a hallmark bridge domain characteristic of the CHITIN PERCEPTION (CHIP) receptor class. Structural analysis of receptor-ligand complexes, biochemistry, and in planta functional studies of inhibitory nanobodies revealed the mechanism of size-selective, high-affinity chitin perception in Lotus japonicus and Medicago truncatula . Additionally, we identified the CHITIN ELICITOR RECEPTOR KINASE (CERK) class as low-affinity, yet essential, co-receptors and propose a mechanistic model for a ligand-induced core signaling heterocomplex. Our findings establish the structural and mechanistic basis of differential chitin perception and receptor complex assembly in chitin-elicited plant immune signaling.

articles_hidden.title: Electrically driven chiral emission from plasmonic tunnel junctions
articles_hidden.authors: Yuanyang Xie, Alexey V. Krasavin, Anatoly V. Zayats
articles_hidden.abstract: Chirality plays a crucial role in a broad range of processes, including light-matter interactions in physics, chemistry, and biology, while quantum tunneling provides a promising mechanism for light generation at the nanoscale. By integrating tunnel junctions with chiral plasmonic nanohelicoids, we achieved electrically induced nanoscale generation of chiral light at the single-particle level. The tunneling-driven resonant excitation of chiral dipolar modes of the nanohelicoids results in emission of a vortex light beam possessing both spin angular momentum with handedness selectivity of more than 0.8 and orbital angular momentum equal in magnitude and opposite in sign. Our electrically driven approach offers a means for engineering photon spin generation at the nanoscale, highlighting its potential for next-generation optical components in display applications, as well as quantum information processing and photochemistry.

articles_hidden.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a universal gate set, but the necessary non-Clifford gates represent a significant resource cost for most quantum error correction architectures. Magic state cultivation offers an efficient alternative to resource-intensive distillation protocols; however, testing the proposal’s assumptions represents a challenging departure from quantum memory experiments. We present an experimental study of magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor. We implement cultivation, including code-switching into a surface code, and develop a fault-tolerant measurement protocol to bound the magic state fidelity. Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40, with a state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1) (retaining 8% of attempts). Our results experimentally establish magic state cultivation as a viable solution to one of quantum computing’s most important challenges.

articles_hidden.title: A pair of chitosan receptors confer broad-spectrum fungal resistance
articles_hidden.authors: Keyi Huang, Jingni Wu, Yu Cao, Yingying Cao, Zhongji Pu, Aoshen Xu, Wenzhao Wang, Xue Zhou, Ming Li, Min Zhang, Yuhua Wang, Jinbiao Ma, Yulin Du, Qin Wang, Yingqiao Wan, Shangyu Gao, Dacheng Wang, Guangzheng Sun, Qin Gu, Huan Chen, Guosheng Xiong, Heng Yin, Yiwen Deng, Wensheng Zhao, Zhengguang Zhang, Shengben Li, Xiquan Gao, Sun Tae Kim, Gang Li, Baolei Jia, Jijie Chai, Kenichi Tsuda, Zheng Qing Fu, Yiming Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Chitosan, a major fungal cell wall component, activates plant immunity, yet the underlying perception mechanism remains unknown. In this study, we identified OsFID1, an apoplast-localized DUF26 domain protein, as a chitosan-binding receptor essential for chitosan-triggered immunity. OsFID1 forms a receptor complex with OsFID2, a plasma membrane–localized DUF26 receptor-like kinase, to mediate chitosan sensing and immune activation, requiring OsFID2 phosphorylation for function. The OsFID1-OsFID2 complex confers broad-spectrum resistance to fungal pathogens. OsFID1 homologs are conserved in land plants, which show chitosan-binding activity in both monocots and dicots. Ectopic expression of OsFID1 in wheat and maize enhanced fungal resistance without growth penalty. These findings uncover a conserved receptor complex for direct chitosan sensing, advancing our understanding of plant-fungus interactions and providing a potential strategy for engineering durable fungal resistance crops.

articles_hidden.title: Empirical constraints on ice cliff calving
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Needell, Catherine C. Walker, Jeremy N. Bassis
articles_hidden.abstract: When calving cliffs at the margins of Earth’s ice sheets exceed a critical height, runaway retreat may be initiated in a process called the marine ice cliff instability. However, sufficiently tall ice cliffs have rarely been observed. To address this gap, we measured the characteristics of 15,330 ice cliffs across Earth’s ice sheet margins using laser altimetry. We show that cliff height is highly correlated with mélange thickness, water depth, and crevassing. We found that tall cliffs calve more rapidly than parameterizations assume, but dynamic thinning and retreat into regions with low ice thickness gradients prevent runaway retreat. These observations suggest that model projections may underestimate subannual rates of cliff calving, but that the potential for instability will depend sensitively on additional quantities, not cliff height alone.

articles_hidden.abstract: Fuel economy matters to both animals and machines, as the cost of transport can determine where, when, and how far locomotion is possible. However, established estimates of these values for animal flight come from laboratories and treat the atmosphere as constant, even though free-flying animals routinely extract energy from atmospheric flows. Using high-resolution movement data, we estimate the cost of transport for 50 bird and bat species flying in the wild. Our results revise the classic ranking of locomotion costs, suggesting that flying can be cheaper than swimming though almost as costly as running, depending on interactions between physical environment, morphology, and behavior. Linking transport costs to atmospheric conditions provides a mechanistic basis for predicting how changing windscapes will reshape the energetics, movements, and distributions of flying animals.

articles_hidden.title: Modular van der Waals MOSFETs through layer-by-layer chalcogen substitutions
articles_hidden.authors: Seok Young Min, Hyunje Cho, Suk-Ho Lee, Jaeho Choi, Taeho Kim, Jong Yun Choi, Heewon Park, Junsoo Yoon, TaeJoon Mo, Chumki Nayak, Gi-Yeop Kim, Sung-Hyuk Her, Chul-Ho Lee, Yong-Sung Kim, Si-Young Choi, Cheol-Joo Kim, Moon-Ho Jo
articles_hidden.abstract: In two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), the local electrostatic field of the chalcogen p -orbitals dictates the crystal field splitting of the transition metal d -orbitals, stabilizing diverse electronic states from semiconducting and semimetallic to exotic topological phases. On-demand substitution of the lattice chalcogens is therefore an efficient route to tuning TMDC electronic phases. Here, we custom-molded van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures by layer-by-layer vapor-phase chalcogen substitution starting from p -type WSe 2 multilayers into which we locally inscribed insulating WO x , n -type WS 2 , and semimetallic WTe 2 . This spatially precise conversion seamlessly integrated distinct electronic phases, both vertically and laterally, into modular vdW semiconductor heterostructures that are otherwise inaccessible. As a demonstration, we integrated WO x /WSe 2 local gate stacks to build ultrascaled metal oxide–semiconductor field effect transistors (MOSFETs), achieving an unprecedented subthreshold swing at subnanometer equivalent oxide thickness.

articles_hidden.title: Regulation of target gene expression by chromatin-associated protein-coding transcripts in plants
articles_hidden.authors: Lu Han, Yuxiang Yuan, Yujie Liu, Yan Li, Yijun Qi
articles_hidden.abstract: Protein-coding transcripts are regarded as intermediates that mediate DNA-to-protein information flow, leaving their noncoding regulatory potential largely underappreciated. Genome-wide profiling of RNA–chromatin interactions in Arabidopsis has uncovered widespread associations between protein-coding transcripts and distinct genomic loci, implying that they possess regulatory functions. Here, we found that BT2 and GSL8 transcripts modulate target gene transcription independently of their protein products through distinct mechanisms. The BT2 transcript represses transcription of its targets CEP2 and MRF4 by forming RNA–DNA triplexes, thereby restricting root growth and promoting flowering, whereas GSL8 acts through a triplex-independent pathway. Our findings unveil intrinsic regulatory activities of protein-coding transcripts, challenging the canonical definition of mRNA function and blurring the functional distinction between coding and noncoding RNAs in the context of genome evolution.

articles_hidden.title: Dendritic computation for abstract rule-based flexible decision-making
articles_hidden.authors: Yuan Zhang, Yanhe Liu, Yachuang Hu, Zhenkun Zhang, Jie Du, Lele Cui, Qi Liu, Lin Zhong, Yu Xin, Ruiming Chai, Li Deng, Jingwei Pan, Jackie Schiller, Ning-long Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: Intelligent behavior involves flexible integration of sensory input and abstract rule knowledge. Dendritic computation has been shown to contribute to top-down modulation of sensory processing; however, whether and how it is involved in flexible cognitive processing remains to be elucidated. Combining a rule-based flexible decision-making task with in vivo two-photon imaging and optogenetics in mice, we found that within single layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the auditory cortex, apical dendrites preferentially encoded the inferred abstract rule and somata preferentially represented sensory stimuli, whereas choice signals were present in both compartments. Optogenetic dendritic inhibition impaired rule-dependent somatic choice coding, supporting a task-relevant integration across the dendritic and somatic compartments. These results indicate that dendritic computation in cortical neurons mediates flexible behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Atomic functional site scaffolding in biopolymers with RFdiffusion3
articles_hidden.authors: Jasper Butcher, Rohith Krishna, Raktim Mitra, Seth M. Woodbury, Donghyo Kim, Rafael I. Brent, Yanjing Li, Nathaniel Corley, Andrew Favor, Anqi Chen, Paul T. Hardy, Bo Qiang, Kieran Didi, Maxwell Kazman, Lars L. Schaaf, Frank DiMaio, David Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: The catalytic and other sophisticated functions of biomolecules arise from the placement of many atoms in three-dimensional space. Here, we describe a generative artificial intelligence method for biopolymers, RFdiffusion3 (RFD3), which employs free atom diffusion to satisfy complex sets of atomic constraints more rapidly and accurately than previous methods across several challenges from enzyme design to RNA structure design. We demonstrate experimentally the power of the RFD3 pipeline for enzyme design by designing de novo phosphotriesterases with a complex active site architecture incorporating a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions and zinc proteases specific for the transthyretin protein involved in amyloid diseases; in both cases we obtain active catalysts in zero shot 96 construct design campaigns.

articles_hidden.title: Gate-tunable chiral spin mode in WSe 2 /WS 2 moiré superlattices
articles_hidden.authors: Zhexu Shan, Wenjian Su, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Shiyao Zhu, Yuanfeng Xu, Yanhao Tang
articles_hidden.abstract: The interplay between many-body and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) effects can lead to previously unobserved phenomena in solids. Chiral spin modes (CSMs) are collective spin excitations that arise from such interplay and connect states with opposite chirality. Here, we report a gate-tunable CSM that occurs between conduction SOC-split minibands in near-0°-twisted WSe 2 /WS 2 bilayers. This mode manifests as a sharp resonance with giant Raman efficiency in the pseudovector-symmetry channel of the Raman spectra. By varying the filling, the CSM transitions from a chiral spin exciton to an excitonic polaron. The spin-flip nature is directly confirmed by the Zeeman effect, and the filling dependence indicates a charge-transfer insulator at unity filling. Our results demonstrate that transition metal–dichalcogenide moiré superlattices are a fertile platform for exploring exotic low-lying collective excitations.

articles_hidden.title: Frequency encoding regulates cell type composition in the small intestine
articles_hidden.authors: Sonja D. C. Weterings, Hiromune Eto, Jan-Daniël de Leede-Scheven, Amir Giladi, Jooske L. Monster, Mirjam E. Hoekstra, Wouter F. Beijk, Esther J. M. Liefting, Karen B. van den Anker, Jacco van Rheenen, Alexander van Oudenaarden, Katharina F. Sonnen
articles_hidden.abstract: Intestinal homeostasis requires tight regulation of stem cell maintenance and differentiation to absorptive and secretory cell types, two major intestinal lineages. Key signaling pathways have been identified, but how they balance cell type composition remains unclear. We uncovered oscillatory expression of the Notch-target protein Hes1 (hairy and enhancer of split 1) that controls cell fate specification in a frequency-dependent manner. An endogenous fluorescent Hes1 reporter revealed distinct, cell type–specific oscillation frequencies forming a gradient along the crypt-villus axis, which was modulated by cell cycle phase as well as Wnt (wingless-related integration site)–signaling and Notch-signaling activity. We developed a microfluidic system to modulate Notch-signaling oscillations in organoids and found the oscillation frequency to regulate the balance of cell type composition. This study provides evidence that information for cell fate specification is encoded in the frequency of an oscillatory signal.

articles_hidden.title: Engineering ordered two-dimensional defect phases to strengthen structural alloys
articles_hidden.authors: Andreas Bezold, Manuel Köbrich, Jan Vollhüter, Longsheng Feng, Lukas Amon, Nicolas Karpstein, Yunzhi Wang, Erdmann Spiecker, Mathias Göken, Michael J. Mills, Steffen Neumeier
articles_hidden.abstract: Defects in crystals are usually considered to be consequences of deformation, but they can also be engineered as strengthening features. Planar defects can strengthen structural alloys but usually form only during deformation or service, limiting control over their density, stability, and chemistry. We show that predeformation followed by aging can convert such defects into a designed architecture of ordered defect phases. In a single-crystal cobalt-nickel–based superalloy and a polycrystalline cobalt-chromium-tungsten alloy, this treatment creates dense networks of coherent, atomically thin, ordered defect–confined phases. These increase room-temperature strength by more than 200 megapascals and reduce the superalloy’s minimum creep rate by more than threefold. Electron microscopy and simulations show that local chemical ordering amplifies strengthening and that the ordered defect phases remain shearable while impeding slip transmission.

articles_hidden.title: Deterministic generation and distribution of genuine multipartite entanglement in macroscopic acoustic resonators
articles_hidden.authors: Dian Tan, Guixu Xie, Libo Zhang, Yang Xu, Chilong Liu, Haolan Yuan, Zhihua Chen, Chang-Kang Hu, J. Q. You, Song Liu, Eric Lutz, Tobias J. Kippenberg, Dapeng Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Generating complex multimode entanglement is a central goal of quantum information science. However, scalable creation of genuine multipartite entanglement is challenging as it requires excellent control and efficient state verification. We report the generation and transfer of genuine multimode entanglement across two multimode acoustic resonators. We prepare genuine multipartite entangled states involving two, four, and six modes across the resonators with respective fidelities of 0.912 ± 0.003, 0.790 ± 0.003, and 0.570 ± 0.001. We further demonstrate the transfer of two- and four-mode genuine entangled states between the resonators with fidelities of 0.785 ± 0.006 and 0.601 ± 0.006. This hardware-efficient and scalable architecture enables deterministic control and generation of complex multimode mechanical states. Our results push the boundary of quantum control in macroscopic mechanical systems, establishing a pathway toward large-scale mechanical quantum networks.

articles_hidden.title: Stereoselective polysubstituted bicyclo[1.1.0]butane synthesis by rhodium-catalyzed kinetic resolution
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaolong Zhang, Rongkai Wu, Zhaohong Liu, Ge Yin, Jiaqi Tang, Paramasivam Sivaguru, Xin Hong, Edward A. Anderson, Xihe Bi
articles_hidden.abstract: Bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) are a distinctive class of strained small-ring carbocycles of growing importance in synthetic and medicinal chemistry. However, the enantioselective synthesis of polysubstituted BCBs remains a largely unsolved challenge. In this study, we report a general chemical platform for the stereoselective assembly of chiral or meso 1,2,3,4-tetrasubstituted BCBs from internal alkynes and carbenes through stepwise [2+1+1’] or one-pot [2+1+1] cycloaddition reactions, respectively. Successful execution of these transformations exploits the combination of triftosylhydrazones (carbene precursors) and chiral dirhodium catalysts. The sterically hindered catalyst Rh 2 ( R -3,5- di PheTPCP) 4 features a confined chiral microenvironment that enables exquisite discrimination between cyclopropene enantiomers, affording highly enantioenriched polysubstituted BCBs through kinetic resolution upon reaction with chiral rhodium carbenes. This chemistry operates under mild reaction conditions, uses readily available starting materials, and exhibits broad substrate scope.

articles_hidden.authors: Pedro Jiménez-Sandoval, Owen Kentish, Caroline Broyart, Hyun Kyung Lee, Klara Culjak, Uwe Osswald, Meriem Aitouguinane, Emanuele Tettamanti, Manon Schmidli, Lu Zhang, Louis-Philippe Maier, Charles Roussin-Léveillée, Diego José Berlanga, Marina Martin-Dacal, Miguel Angel Torres, Varun Kumar, Patricia Fernández-Calvo, José M. Jimenez-Gomez, Philippe Reymond, Alberto P. Macho, Fabian Pfrengle, Lucía Jordá, Antonio Molina, Julia Santiago
articles_hidden.abstract: Pathogens target and degrade the extracellular matrix surrounding plant cells. A central question is how cell wall–derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) are recognized and integrated to trigger immune responses. We address this question by determining the structure of the extracellular multidomain of the impaired in glycan perception 1 (IGP1) receptor in both apo form and bound to the cellulose-derived DAMP cellotriose. Structural analyses reveal that constitutive interactions of leucine-rich repeat (LRR)–malectin domains preconfigure IGP1 for ligand recognition and that the receptor features a highly specific sugar-binding pocket in the LRR domain capable of distinguishing fine variations in glycan structures. By directly sensing cello-oligomers, IGP1 operates as a cell wall surveillance receptor that links pathogen-induced wall degradation to immune alerting, equipping plants to mount rapid and robust defense responses.

articles_hidden.title: In situ structure of the human ciliary transition zone links linker defects to primary ciliary dyskinesia
articles_hidden.authors: Haixia Zhou, Lea Terbeck, Andrew Berical, Marine Brunet, Sven M. Lange, Jacob R. Anderson, Heike Olbrich, Diana Carolin Bracht, Kai Wohlgemuth, Cynthia Rieck, Johanna Raidt, Jürgen Klingauf, Sivagurunathan Sutharsan, Huda Mussaffi, Dario Prais, Victoria Dunphy, Sachiko T. Homma, Paul Guichard, Virginie Hamel, Finn J. Hawkins, Heymut Omran, Alan Brown
articles_hidden.abstract: The ciliary transition zone (TZ) regulates ciliary proteome composition, yet its molecular architecture, protein content, and contribution to motile ciliopathies remain poorly defined. We applied in situ cryo–electron tomography and subtomogram averaging to human multiciliated epithelial cells. This approach resolved TZ-specific doublet microtubules at subnanometer resolution and identified nine constituent proteins. We found that epithelial cell transforming 2 like (ECT2L) and double zinc ribbon and ankyrin repeat-containing protein 1 (DZANK1) form the major linker complexes between adjacent TZ doublet microtubules. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in either gene cause primary ciliary dyskinesia. ECT2L and DZANK1 deficiency disrupted TZ architecture, caused microtubular abnormalities and abnormal bulbous ciliary tips, and impaired mucociliary clearance. These findings establish a direct genetic link between TZ defects and human motile ciliopathy and illustrate how in situ structural biology can uncover mechanisms of human disease.

articles.title: Mesoscale structures in signed networks
articles.authors: Wei Zhang, Olga Boichak, Tristram J. Alexander, Tiago P. Peixoto, Eduardo G. Altmann
articles.abstract: Mesoscale structures in signed networks have been studied under the limiting assumption of the validity of social balance theory, which predicts positive connections within groups and negative connections between groups. Here, we propose and apply a methodology that overcomes this limitation and is able to find and characterize also the different possible unbalanced structures in signed networks. Applying our methodology to 24 empirical networks, from social-political, financial, and biological domains, we find that unbalanced mesoscale structures are prevalent in real-world networks, including cases with substantial balance at the microscale of triangles. In particular, we find that assortativity often prevails regardless of the interaction sign and that core-periphery structures are typical in online social networks. Our findings highlight the complexity of mesoscale relational structures, the importance of using computational methods that are a priori agnostic to specific patterns, and the importance of independently evaluating micro- and mesoscale predictions of social balance theory.

articles.title: How inequality became durable before states: Evidence from 6000 years in the Central Plain of China
articles.authors: Dongdong Li, Suwei Guo, Xingcan Chen
articles.abstract: How did durable inequality emerge before the rise of states? Drawing on a synthesis of previously published mortuary data from more than 2300 burials, together with isotopic, zooarchaeological, and osteological data spanning nearly 6000 years (7000 to 1500 BCE) in the prehistoric Central Plain of China, we reconstruct long-term patterns of relational mortuary inequality. We show that inequality followed a strongly nonlinear trajectory and cannot be explained primarily by agricultural intensification or population scale. Instead, substantial disparities were structured by differential positions within social-relational networks that mediated access to labor, resources, and symbolic capital. Transformations in subsistence, the rise of mobile and appropriable wealth, and escalating conflict reorganized these networks, concentrating ritual and political-military power and technological control. Early states stabilized rather than created these preexisting disparities by institutionalizing control over resources, violence, and network-based access. These findings highlight the central role of social networks in shaping durable inequality before formal state institutions.
